definition: In this historical usage, an ultimate cause is the highest or last explanatory source to which other causes are traced back. In the Aristotelian discussion in the packet, it is linked with ultimate final cause and treated as the source of all motion.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Cause and Effect; pinned source text

reasons: The definition’s phrase “highest or last explanatory source” is not explicitly supported by the packet text provided.

While the packet does state that Aristotle’s ultimate final cause was regarded as also the ultimate cause of all motion, it does not define “ultimate cause” as “the highest or last explanatory source” in general terms.

The definition’s wording that it is “treated as the source of all motion” is supported only in the specific Aristotelian discussion noted in the packet, but the rest of the definition overgeneralizes beyond what the packet directly says.
The opening gloss, “the highest or last explanatory source to which other causes are traced back,” is an unsupported generalization not stated in the packet.

The packet supports only the Aristotelian link between “ultimate final cause” and “the ultimate cause of all motion”; it does not support a broader historical definition of “ultimate cause” in general.
